transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Yeah, um… thanks, Doctor. I guess I’m here because I’ve just been feeling kind of… constantly revved up, like I’m running hot all the time. Like I can’t really shut the motor off, if that makes sense.

I’ve tried to just push through it — especially at the firehouse, you know, that job kind of expects you to be ready to go — but lately it’s been starting to cause some problems there. Nothing I’m proud of. I just figured maybe I should talk to somebody before it gets worse.
How long have you been feeling this constantly 'revved up,' and did it start suddenly after a particular event, or has it built up gradually over time?

Um… I’d say it’s been a real problem for maybe a year and five months or so. It wasn’t like one big event where I changed overnight, at least I don’t think so.

It kind of built up after our shifts got longer and started rotating more, and then they added more documentation and the drone duties. I kept telling myself, “That’s just the job, just adapt,” you know? But around then is when it started feeling like I couldn’t really come down from it anymore. Does that make sense?
Has there been a specific incident at work—like a call or event you witnessed—that felt life-threatening or deeply traumatic to you, which you can point to as connected to how you've been feeling?

I don’t think so… not one specific call, anyway. I mean, we see rough stuff sometimes, that’s part of it, but I can’t point to one incident where I felt like, “That’s when this started.”

It feels more like it’s been the pace and the buildup, if that makes sense. But no, I don’t think there was one life-threatening or traumatic event I’m connecting it to.

Do you ever have sudden episodes where, out of nowhere, you get hit with intense fear or panic along with things like a racing heart, chest tightness, or shortness of breath that peak within a few minutes?

Um… I don’t think so. Not like it comes out of nowhere and peaks like that, no.

I mean, I can get worked up, sure, but I wouldn’t call it sudden panic with chest tightness or not being able to breathe. At least not that I’ve noticed. Does that answer what you mean?
Beyond the work stress, do you find yourself worrying excessively about other things too—like your health, finances, family, or other everyday matters—even when there's no clear reason to worry?

Um… I don’t think it’s that broad, no. I mean, I worry about normal stuff—bills, my family, staying healthy—but I wouldn’t say I’m constantly worrying about everything for no reason.

It feels more tied to work and trying to keep up, I guess. At least that’s how it seems to me. Does that make sense?
On your days off, away from the firehouse, do you still feel that same revved-up, can't-shut-off feeling, or does it noticeably ease up when you're not at work?

It eases a little when I’m not actually at the firehouse, but… not as much as I’d like to say. I still feel kind of revved up, like my motor’s running even when there’s nothing I have to be doing.

I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but that’s kind of why I’m here. I feel like I’m always running hot, and lately it’s been spilling over enough that it’s causing problems at work. Does that answer it?
When you do get a chance to unwind, do you find it hard to actually control or stop that keyed-up, worried feeling once it starts, even when you consciously try to relax?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I do try to relax, and sometimes it helps a bit, but I don’t know if I’d say I “can’t control it” exactly.

It’s more like… I have a hard time settling down, if that makes sense. But I don’t want to overstate it. I can usually get through it. I just don’t always feel like I actually unwind the way I’m supposed to. Is that what you’re asking?
Have you been having trouble with sleep lately—like difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up feeling rested—separate from how busy or worried you feel?

I’m not really sure how to separate that out, honestly. My sleep isn’t perfect, but I’ve kind of always chalked that up to the job schedule or just having a lot on my mind.

I don’t know that I’d say there’s a clear sleep problem on its own, if that makes sense. I can try to pay closer attention to it, though, if that would help.
Have you noticed physical tension, like muscle tightness, or increased irritability and being easily annoyed, that's been happening along with this revved-up feeling?

I’m not sure I’ve really tracked that, to be honest. I mean, I probably get tense like anyone does, especially after a long stretch, but I haven’t noticed a clear muscle-tightness thing that stands out.

As far as being annoyed… I don’t know. I’d like to think I’m not snapping at people or anything. Maybe I get a little short sometimes, but I’m not sure if that’s tied to the revved-up feeling or just normal stress. Does that make sense?
Have you noticed any trouble concentrating or your mind going blank, especially when you're trying to focus on tasks either at work or at home?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m not paying attention on purpose or anything, but that does happen.

Like in briefings, or when we’re doing drone training, I’ll be locked in for the first few minutes, and then I realize I’ve kind of been staring at the map or the screen and I didn’t actually catch half of what command just said. It’s embarrassing, honestly, so I try to cover it by looking back over things or asking someone quietly.

So, yes, concentrating can be hard sometimes—especially if I’m supposed to stay focused on one thing for a while.

If your work situation went back to how it was before the schedule and duty changes—less demanding, no drone duties—do you think this revved-up, on-edge feeling would go away, or do you think it would still be there regardless?

I want to say it would go away, because that would be the easy answer… and maybe it would get better some.

But honestly, I think this is kind of why I’m here. I feel like I’m always running hot, like I can’t really shut the motor off. And lately it’s been showing up at the firehouse enough that it’s getting me in trouble, which is… not great to admit.

So, yes, the schedule and drone stuff probably make it worse, but I’m not sure it’s only that. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Would you say you've been feeling this keyed-up, worried, hard-to-control tension more days than not over the past six months, even before the recent schedule changes made things worse?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s been a real problem for, I guess, about a year and five months now.

It really started getting noticeable after the longer rotating shifts came in, and then the extra documentation and the drone duties got added on top of that. The recent changes definitely made it worse, but it wasn’t just the last few weeks or anything like that. It’s been going on a while.

Compared to how your colleagues seem to be handling these same schedule and duty changes, would you say your reaction feels a lot more intense or harder to manage than theirs, or is it in the same ballpark as what everyone else is dealing with?

I’d like to say it’s the same as everyone else, because nobody’s exactly thrilled about the changes… but if I’m being honest, I think mine’s been harder to manage.

Other guys seem irritated or tired, but they’re still keeping the details straight. With me, it’s started costing me trust at the firehouse. I got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which was… pretty humiliating. And I was hoping to move toward a leadership role, but now it feels like that’s slipping because the crew can’t really count on me to track things consistently.

I hate saying that out loud, but… yeah, I think it’s more than just normal stress.

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: In briefings or drone training, I’m locked in for the first few minutes, then I realize I’ve been staring at the map or the screen and didn’t catch half of what command just said.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble concentrating or going blank while trying to focus on tasks, which most directly matches difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m not paying attention on purpose or anything, but that does happen.

Like in briefings, or when we’re doing drone training, I’ll be locked in for the first few minutes, and then I realize I’ve kind of been staring at the map or the screen and I didn’t actually catch half of what command just said. It’s embarrassing, honestly, so I try to cover it by looking back over things or asking someone quietly.

So, yes, concentrating can be hard sometimes—especially if I’m supposed to stay focused on one thing for a while.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the anxiety is directly tied to and would resolve with removal of the specific work stressor (supporting adjustment disorder) versus persisting independently of the stressor (supporting GAD)
doctor.question: If your work situation went back to how it was before the schedule and duty changes—less demanding, no drone duties—do you think this revved-up, on-edge feeling would go away, or do you think it would still be there regardless?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I feel like I’m always running hot, like I can’t shut the motor off, and lately that’s been getting me in trouble at the firehouse.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the ongoing revved-up, on-edge feeling would persist even if work demands decreased, which most directly matches the constant 'driven by a motor' feeling.

patient.answer:
I want to say it would go away, because that would be the easy answer… and maybe it would get better some.

But honestly, I think this is kind of why I’m here. I feel like I’m always running hot, like I can’t really shut the motor off. And lately it’s been showing up at the firehouse enough that it’s getting me in trouble, which is… not great to admit.

So, yes, the schedule and drone stuff probably make it worse, but I’m not sure it’s only that. Does that answer what you’re asking?

inference.note: No new information ruling in/out either diagnosis; symptoms remain closely tied to work stressor without full pervasive worry pattern, but some GAD-like features (concentration difficulty, restlessness) persist, keeping both adjustment disorder and GAD as candidates.

doctor.intent: Determine if the excessive worry/on-edge feeling has been present more days than not for at least 6 months, a key duration criterion for GAD (F41.1) versus adjustment disorder (F43.23)
doctor.question: Would you say you've been feeling this keyed-up, worried, hard-to-control tension more days than not over the past six months, even before the recent schedule changes made things worse?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It’s been a real problem for about a year and five months, ever since the longer rotating shifts and extra documentation and drone duties got added.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long and how consistently the keyed-up feeling has been present, especially whether it has lasted more than six months.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s been a real problem for, I guess, about a year and five months now.

It really started getting noticeable after the longer rotating shifts came in, and then the extra documentation and the drone duties got added on top of that. The recent changes definitely made it worse, but it wasn’t just the last few weeks or anything like that. It’s been going on a while.

inference.note: Chronicity beyond 6 months, some persistence even off-duty, and partial uncontrollability support GAD; however, worry remains largely work-focused and tied to identifiable stressor onset, keeping adjustment disorder in consideration, though less likely given failure to resolve when stressor eases.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the anxiety and distress are markedly out of proportion to the work stressor (suggesting adjustment disorder) versus a more generalized, pervasive pattern not fully explained by the stressor's severity (suggesting GAD)
doctor.question: Compared to how your colleagues seem to be handling these same schedule and duty changes, would you say your reaction feels a lot more intense or harder to manage than theirs, or is it in the same ballpark as what everyone else is dealing with?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: This has started costing me trust at the firehouse; I was pulled into a performance and safety meeting, and now my shot at moving into leadership feels like it’s slipping because the crew can’t count on me to track the details consistently.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether his reaction to the same work stressors is more intense or harder to manage than colleagues', which relates most directly to whether the symptoms are causing noticeable impairment at work beyond normal stress.

patient.answer:
I’d like to say it’s the same as everyone else, because nobody’s exactly thrilled about the changes… but if I’m being honest, I think mine’s been harder to manage.

Other guys seem irritated or tired, but they’re still keeping the details straight. With me, it’s started costing me trust at the firehouse. I got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which was… pretty humiliating. And I was hoping to move toward a leadership role, but now it feels like that’s slipping because the crew can’t really count on me to track things consistently.

I hate saying that out loud, but… yeah, I think it’s more than just normal stress.

inference.note: Symptoms have persisted more days than not for over a year, involve difficulty controlling worry/tension, concentration problems, and are described as more intense than typical stress reactions among peers, fitting GAD criteria. The patient also acknowledges the symptoms might not fully resolve even if the work stressor were removed, arguing against Adjustment Disorder (F43.23), which is now ruled out given the chronicity, pervasiveness, and lack of clear resolution tied strictly to the stressor.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit / chief complaint
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a persistent, difficult-to-control 'revved up' feeling present more days than not for approximately 17 months, occurring across contexts (not confined solely to work), with associated concentration difficulty and functional impairment (performance/safety issues, jeopardized promotion). Symptoms are excessive relative to peers facing the same stressor, arguing against a normative stress reaction. No discrete panic attacks (ruling out F41.0), no identifiable trauma/life-threatening event (ruling out PTSD/adjustment disorder given duration exceeds typical adjustment disorder timeframe and lacks a specific stressor onset), and worry is not broad/multi-domain in the classic GAD sense but is chronic, hard to control, and accompanied by concentration issues and subjective tension—supporting Generalized Anxiety Disorder given the pervasive, uncontrollable, duration-based presentation.
